sourceReviews.supportingSummary: Independently read the actual OPENJSON (Transact-SQL) MCP receipt, concentrating on WITH syntax, colName/type/column_path, AS JSON, its worked nested Order example and Remarks. AS JSON selects an inner object or array as a JSON fragment and specifically requires nvarchar(MAX). Without the flag an explicit-schema column performs scalar extraction; increasing its text capacity does not change the scalar-versus-fragment contract, and default lax mode gives NULL for the unavailable scalar at an object-valued path. The example demonstrates both typed nested scalar columns, including an INT at $.Item.Quantity, and an nvarchar(max) AS JSON column preserving the full Order object. These contracts directly distinguish all four proposed definitions. The article applies to SQL Server 2016 and later and gives the ordinary compatibility threshold of 130, satisfied by the stated SQL Server 2022/160 scope. Neither the newer compatibility override nor the Synapse-only identity feature is part of this item.

choiceReviews.rationale: Inserted literally, detail nvarchar(max) '$.detail' AS JSON follows the documented order colName, type, column_path, AS JSON. The existing $.detail value is an object, so SELECT detail FROM OPENJSON(@payload) WITH (detail nvarchar(max) '$.detail' AS JSON); yields one detail column containing the object {"items":2,"memo":"ship"}, rather than separate child fields. nvarchar(max) is also the required type when AS JSON is specified. Literal positive alternative: with @payload = N'{"detail":[{"items":2},{"items":1}]}', the identical SELECT preserves the array [{"items":2},{"items":1}] as the fragment. The AS JSON argument contract explicitly permits both object and array fragments, and its worked Order projection corroborates object preservation.

detail nvarchar(max) '$.detail' omits AS JSON, so it requests a scalar at an object-valued path. Default lax projection returns SQL NULL, not the serialized object; nvarchar(max) specifies text capacity, not fragment eligibility. The primary AS JSON section distinguishes these cases and requires the flag for a nested fragment. Literal positive countercontext: with @payload = N'{"detail":"ship"}', SELECT detail FROM OPENJSON(@payload) WITH (detail nvarchar(max) '$.detail'); returns the scalar text ship. In that alternative the exact proposed column definition is the appropriate scalar projection because detail is a JSON string, not an object.

detail int '$.detail.items' follows the existing nested scalar path and yields the integer 2. It discards memo and the enclosing object and also violates the required nvarchar(max) output type. This is a wrong result contract, not invalid T-SQL. Literal positive countercontext with the original JSON unchanged: if a downstream step needs only the item count, SELECT detail FROM OPENJSON(@payload) WITH (detail int '$.detail.items'); returns the desired count 2 as int. The article's typed-column definition and its Quantity INT '$.Item.Quantity' example support precisely this scalar numeric projection.

detail nvarchar(max) '$.detail.memo' extracts the string ship, not the complete detail object. Its SQL text type meets the requested type but its selected JSON value does not meet the required structure; items and the object boundary are lost. Literal positive countercontext with the original input: when the consumer requires the memo text alone, SELECT detail FROM OPENJSON(@payload) WITH (detail nvarchar(max) '$.detail.memo'); returns ship and is correct for that task. The column_path and scalar-projection contracts, illustrated by nested text columns in the article, support both this valid use and its insufficiency for the original whole-object requirement.
